summary: Between minute 0 and 27 of the window, backlog grew while arrival rate stayed normal, so the queue stall is a service-rate failure on the consumer side, not a demand surge: consumer throughput fell roughly 40% over the same interval. Two changes landed in the preceding hour (a consumer-library upgrade and a database index rebuild), and consumer logs carry one degradation signature plausibly tied to each (rising lock-waits, rising deserialization warnings). Both signatures draw on the same per-message processing budget, so either alone, or both additively, could account for the throughput loss. Throughput recovered only after both changes were reverted together; no single-change revert was ever run, no traces were retained, and telemetry cannot separate database wait time from deserialization retry time. The change set as a whole is therefore well supported as the cause, while attribution to either individual change is unresolved and cannot be settled from the evidence in hand. The highest-leverage control point is a staged re-application or partial revert that breaks the confounding, backed by instrumentation that splits the two wait categories; scaling or backpressure can relieve the backlog but does not discriminate between causes.

claims.statement: Request arrival rate remained within its normal range throughout the degradation window, so demand-side load increase is not a contributor.
Consumer throughput fell by roughly 40% during the window; this reduced service rate is the proximate mechanism of the stall.
Queue depth rose steadily for 27 minutes; the growing backlog is the observed outcome, a symptom of the service-rate deficit rather than a cause.
Two changes entered the system within the preceding hour - a consumer-library upgrade and a database index rebuild - giving two candidate contributors that are temporally coincident with each other.
Consumer logs show an increase in lock-wait messages during the window, indicating consumers spent additional time blocked on contended resources.
Consumer logs show an increase in message-deserialization warnings during the window, indicating additional or repeated decode work per message.
The index rebuild is a candidate contributor acting through database-side contention that surfaces to consumers as lock-wait time.
The consumer-library upgrade is a candidate contributor acting through changed deserialization behavior that adds retry or fallback work per message.
Reverting both changes together restored throughput, which supports the combined change set as causally responsible for the throughput loss.

Attribution to either individual change is unresolved: the revert was joint, no partial-revert run exists, no traces were retained, and telemetry does not separate database wait from deserialization retry.
Both candidate mechanisms consume the same per-message processing budget, so their effects may be additive and no single-cause assumption is warranted.
The instrumentation gap is itself a contributor to the outcome's duration: with no time-split telemetry and no retained traces, the degradation could not be localized while it ran.

relationships.rationale: Both changes landed in the hour before the throughput decline began.
Database contention consumes consumer processing time, lowering service rate.
Extra deserialization work consumes the same per-message budget, lowering service rate.
With arrival rate steady, a reduced drain rate produces monotonic backlog growth.
Throughput loss is the intermediate mechanism through which the changes reach queue depth.
Normal arrival rate rules out demand growth and isolates the service side.
Lock-wait growth is the log signature expected of database-side contention.
Deserialization warnings are the log signature expected of changed decode behavior.
Recovery on joint revert ties the outcome to the change set, without resolving which member.
Relative share, interaction, or dominance between the two candidates cannot be determined from the evidence.
Confounded revert and absent traces prevent the recovery observation from narrowing to one change.
Additivity is plausible from shared budget but has no direct measurement behind it.
Inability to localize the slowdown while it ran extended the interval over which backlog accumulated.

uncertainties.statement: Which change caused the throughput loss, or whether both did, is unresolved; the surviving alternatives are library-only, rebuild-only, and both-additive.
uncertainties.missingEvidence: A run in which exactly one change is reverted or re-applied (E7 states none exists).

uncertainties.statement: The share of lost processing time attributable to database waiting versus deserialization retry cannot be apportioned.
uncertainties.missingEvidence: Telemetry that splits the two wait categories (E5), or retained trace samples (E8).

uncertainties.statement: The two log signatures are assumed to map to the index rebuild and the library upgrade respectively, but the mapping is inferred from co-timing, not measured.
uncertainties.missingEvidence: Per-signature attribution linking log volume to a specific change.

uncertainties.statement: A third, unrecorded change or environmental shift coinciding with the window and with the revert cannot be excluded.
uncertainties.missingEvidence: A complete inventory of changes and environment state across the window; the package lists only two changes.

uncertainties.statement: Whether the two mechanisms interact (for example, slower database calls widening a deserialization retry window) rather than merely summing is unknown.
uncertainties.missingEvidence: Per-stage timing under each change in isolation.

uncertainties.statement: Whether the increased log messages reflect a rate increase per message or the same rate over retried messages is not distinguished, so severity per message is unclear.
uncertainties.missingEvidence: Per-message counters normalized by processed volume.

uncertainties.statement: It is unknown whether the 40% throughput loss scales with consumer concurrency, which determines whether capacity changes would have relieved or worsened contention.
uncertainties.missingEvidence: Throughput measured at more than one consumer concurrency level during the window.

actions.action: Re-apply the two changes one at a time, in separate windows, measuring consumer throughput after each, so the confound is broken by construction.
actions.rationale: Directly produces the single-change observation that E7 says is missing, and is the only step that can resolve U1 with evidence rather than inference.

actions.action: Instrument the consumer to report time spent waiting on the database separately from time spent in deserialization and its retries.
actions.rationale: Closes the gap named in E5; on its own it changes nothing about throughput, but without it no future run can apportion loss between the two mechanisms.

actions.action: Retain trace samples continuously, or at minimum during and after change windows, rather than discarding them.
actions.rationale: E8 shows the absence of traces removed the per-request path evidence that would have localized the stall while it was running.

actions.action: Prohibit overlapping consumer-code and database-maintenance changes in the same window, or stagger them with a measurement gap between.
actions.rationale: Removes the structural cause of the unresolvable attribution in E3 and E7; it does not address whichever mechanism was actually at fault.

actions.action: Treat added consumer capacity or backpressure as backlog relief only, and confirm throughput scales before relying on it.
actions.rationale: Acts on the outcome in C3 without discriminating causes; under lock contention (C7) added concurrency may not raise throughput, which is the open question in U7.

actions.action: Schedule or throttle index rebuilds so they do not overlap live consumer traffic.
actions.rationale: Effective only if C7 holds; its value depends on the outcome of A1, so it should not be adopted as the fix before attribution.

counterfactuals.premise: If arrival rate had risen outside its normal range during the window.
counterfactuals.expected: Backlog growth would be explainable by demand, and the ~40% throughput drop would need re-examination as a possible saturation effect rather than a capacity loss.
counterfactuals.implication: E1 is what licenses treating this as a service-side failure; the diagnosis rests on it.

counterfactuals.premise: If only the library upgrade had been reverted and throughput had returned to normal.
counterfactuals.expected: The rebuild would be demoted to a coincident non-contributor and the library upgrade confirmed as sufficient cause.
counterfactuals.implication: No such run exists (E7), so no single-change conclusion can be drawn; this is the experiment A1 supplies.

counterfactuals.premise: If only one of the two log signatures had increased.
counterfactuals.expected: A single supported contributor would be the parsimonious reading, and the additive hypothesis would drop out.
counterfactuals.implication: Both signatures rose (E4), so the contributor network must stay two-branched rather than being collapsed for simplicity.

counterfactuals.premise: If traces or split wait-time telemetry had been available for the window.
counterfactuals.expected: The lost processing time could have been apportioned between database wait and deserialization retry, resolving U1 and U2 without any revert experiment.
counterfactuals.implication: The observability gap, not the system's behavior, is what forces the diagnosis to stop at the change-set level.

counterfactuals.premise: If an unrecorded third factor had degraded and recovered on the same timeline as the changes and their revert.
counterfactuals.expected: The recovery in E6 would be coincidental and both candidate contributors would be spurious.
counterfactuals.implication: Nothing in the package excludes this; the joint-revert recovery is strong but not decisive evidence, which caps confidence in C9 at the change-set level.

counterfactuals.premise: If the team selected the library upgrade alone as the control point and permanently rolled it back.
counterfactuals.expected: Recurrence on the next index rebuild if the rebuild was the dominant contributor, with the same unresolved signatures.
counterfactuals.implication: Control-point selection should be the isolation experiment (A1), not a bet on one candidate before attribution exists.
